_meta.name: FlameGuard lessons learned from spacecraft fire incidents
_meta.integrity_rule: Every incident fact, spacecraft hardware item, and microgravity science link cites an official NASA archive source (nasa.gov, ntrs.nasa.gov, appel.nasa.gov, nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov). The 'design_takeaways' section is an interpretive synthesis for research context and is not official NASA operational procedure.
_meta.warning: Educational research content. Not an operational fire-response procedure.

facts.fact: Fire swept the capsule in seconds, fed by about 70 lb of flammable material (nylon netting, Velcro) and pure oxygen.
Opening the hatch took at least 90 seconds, while the fire consumed the cabin oxygen in about 25 seconds.
Investigators concluded an electrical short-circuit or arc near the Environmental Control Unit area was the most probable ignition source, though the exact point of origin could not be pinpointed.

Rapid combustion of the 16.7 psi pure-oxygen cabin atmosphere spiked internal pressure past structural limits, rupturing the command module pressure vessel and preventing the inward-opening hatch from being opened.

changes_made: Ground-test launch-pad atmosphere changed from 100% oxygen to a nitrogen/oxygen mixture (60% O2 / 40% N2 at launch, transitioning to pure oxygen in orbit).
Command Module hatch redesigned to swing outward for rapid crew egress.
Flammable interior materials replaced with self-extinguishing alternatives; electrical wiring and plumbing protected and rerouted.
NASA safety governance and oversight reformed following the AS-204 Review Board and Senate investigation.

incidents.type: Electrically initiated fire inside an oxygen tank (not a cabin fire)

environment.microgravity_relevance: In transit to the Moon; tank fans were used to stir the oxygen.

facts.fact: The Apollo 13 Review Board concluded an electrically initiated fire inside Service Module Oxygen Tank No. 2 caused the accident.
Damaged Teflon insulation on wiring inside the tank shorted and ignited; the fire raised pressure until the tank burst (overpressure, not a chemical explosion).
Heater thermostat switches were welded closed during ground testing; the heater probably reached about 500 C (1,000 F) but the gauge only read up to 85 F, so crews did not notice.
Board recommended redesign of the oxygen storage system and minimizing combustible items inside the tank (done for Apollo 14).

incidents.scope_context: Apollo 13 involved an electrically initiated fire inside a closed oxygen tank rather than an open-cabin flame. It demonstrates the same underlying hazard combination as Apollo 1: high-concentration oxygen, damaged electrical insulation, and an ignition spark.

incidents.type: Fire in orbit (microgravity) from a solid-fuel oxygen generator (Vika/SFOG candle)

facts.fact: A solid-fuel oxygen generator canister burst into flame, shooting a blowtorch-like flame about three feet long with sparks and molten metal and producing dense smoke.
The flame blocked the path to the docked Soyuz escape vehicle.
The candle type had been used more than 2,500 times without incident.
Crew put on masks and fought the fire with foam extinguishers; the station life support cleared smoke over several hours.
Burning metal globules were thrown into microgravity and splattered on the opposite bulkhead.

changes_made: Crew emergency training and ground controller coordination procedures were updated following the Mir incident.
Canister manufacturing quality and fire-resistant shielding were improved; solid-fuel oxygen generators are used on the ISS with added containment measures.
ISS oxygen supply relies on dissimilar redundancy (Elektron units plus the US Oxygen Generation System), keeping SFOG canisters as backup.

iss_fire_safety_hardware.item: Carbon dioxide (CO2) portable fire extinguishers in the US Orbital Segment; water-based foam extinguishers in the Russian Segment
Fine water mist portable fire extinguisher developed to replace Halon-type agents (Halon 1301 phased out under the Montreal Protocol)
Water mist suppression project evaluated droplet size and water mass in ground and free-fall tests (2011–2016) across open-cabin, rack, oxygen candle, and elevated-O2 ISS scenarios

microgravity_fire_science_links.link: No buoyancy: a candle flame burns as a small dim blue sphere around the wick in microgravity, rather than the tall yellow teardrop observed in 1g.
Airflow governs oxygen delivery in orbit: in microgravity, spacecraft ventilation fan speed controls oxygen transport to the flame front, sustaining or quenching combustion.
Low flow can extinguish flames: ISS thin-solid combustion tests quenched when forced flow dropped to 2.2 cm/s at 18.7% O2 (archived in FlameGuard as COMPACT-M3-ISS-THIN-SOLID).

Higher oxygen lowers quenching margins: in BASS-II ISS tests, flame spread rate increased with O2% and low-speed forced flow, while the minimum airflow required to sustain burning decreased at elevated oxygen.

design_takeaways.label: FlameGuard interpretive synthesis of the cited NASA sources. Not official NASA procedure.

items.takeaway: Control both cabin oxygen mole fraction and total pressure; Apollo 1, Apollo 13, and Mir all involved oxygen-rich environments.
Minimize combustible interior materials and qualify spacecraft materials at worst-case cabin O2 and pressure rather than air alone.
Protect electrical wiring insulation in oxygen-rich systems and instrument heaters with sensors that read above nominal limits.
Reducing cabin ventilation can quench open-cabin flames (observed in BASS-II Sample 147 and ISS thin-solid tests) but cannot extinguish self-oxidizing sources such as oxygen candles.
Maintain unobstructed egress paths to return vehicles and provide rapid-opening crew hatches.
Ensure respiratory protection and segment-appropriate fire extinguishers alongside integrated crew and mission-control emergency training.
Interpret 1g flammability test results carefully; absence of buoyancy changes flame geometry, soot production, and sensitivity to forced airflow.

data_gaps: Numerical droplet-size and water-flux tables from the 2011–2016 ISS water mist suppression tests (NTRS 20170009414) are not yet digitized into the FlameGuard SQLite dataset.
Apollo 13 is cataloged as a historical oxygen-tank failure case study rather than an open-cabin microgravity combustion experiment.
Additional NASA PSI investigation CSV/JSON packages can be imported via the Library Data Sources importer when downloaded from individual PSI investigation repositories.
